text: linkedin company/amazon-web-services Amazon Web Services (AWS) Launched in 2006, Amazon Web Services (AWS) began exposing key infrastructure services to businesses in the form of web services -- now widely known as cloud computing. The ultimate benefit of cloud computing, and AWS, is the ability to leverage a new business model and turn capital infrastructure expenses into variable costs. Businesses no longer need to plan and procure servers and other IT resources weeks or months in advance. Using AWS, businesses can take advantage of Amazon's expertise and economies of scale to access resources when their business needs them, delivering results faster and at a lower cost. Today, Amazon Web Services provides a highly reliable, scalable, low-cost infrastructure platform in the cloud that powers hundreds of thousands of businesses in 190 countries around the world. With data center locations in the U.S., Europe, Singapore, and Japan, customers across all industries are taking advantage of our low cost, elastic, open and flexible, secure platform.

Dynatrace provides businesses with a holistic view of their entire digital ecosystem, removing the burden of operational monitoring and alert management. By automating these tasks, teams are empowered to transform complexity into their greatest asset and to drive their business forward by focusing on high-impact initiatives, driving topline acceleration, fueling innovation, and delivering experiences customers love.

title: Abel Berhane
summary: I Code. I Play. I Learn.
text: abelberhane user Abel Berhane I Code. I Play. I Learn. Orlando, FL # Abel Berhane I help teams move from **AI curiosity** to **AI-enabled software delivery**. I work in **GitHub Offerings and AI enablement**, where my focus is turning fast-moving GitHub Copilot and agentic development capabilities into practical material that teams can actually use: workshops, delivery guidance, demos, field notes, governance discussions, and adoption patterns. The work sits at the intersection of **developer productivity**, **enterprise readiness**, **AI-assisted engineering**, and **enablement at scale**. --- ## 🎯 What I am focused on - **GitHub Copilot enablement** — helping engineers and organizations understand where Copilot fits across planning, coding, testing, review, and modernization. - **AI offerings and delivery content** — building and refining workshops, training paths, demos, labs, speaker notes, and reusable delivery assets. - **Agentic development workflows** — exploring how coding agents, MCP, custom instructions, repository context, and automation change the way teams build software. - **Enterprise adoption patterns** — translating governance, security, policy, measurement, and rollout strategy into guidance that is easier for teams to apply. - **Operational quality** — keeping offerings current through review loops, diff tracking, quality checks, release awareness, and structured handoff processes. --- ## 🧩 The kind of problems I like I like the middle between **new AI capability** and **real enterprise usage**. That usually means answering questions like: - Where does this capability fit in the developer workflow? - What should a team try first? - What needs guardrails before it scales? - How do we explain the value without overselling it? - How do we keep training material current when the platform keeps changing? - How do we make adoption measurable, repeatable, and useful for real developers? That is the work I enjoy most: taking something new, technical, and sometimes unclear, then turning it into a path a team can follow. --- ## 🧭 Throughline | Area | What it means to me | | --- | --- | | **AI-assisted development** | Helping teams use AI as part of their workflows, not just as a chat window next to the code. | | **Copilot adoption** | Moving from individual experimentation to team-level practices, governance, and measurable outcomes. | | **Offerings development** | Creating delivery assets that are accurate, usable, current, and easy for other engineers to run. | | **Enterprise readiness** | Balancing speed with security, policy, trust, and operational consistency. | | **Hands-on enablement** | Teaching through examples, demos, exercises, and practical workflow changes. | --- ## 🛠️ How I work I try to keep things practical. The best AI guidance is not just a list of features. It should help a team understand what changed, why it matters, what to try, what to avoid, and how to know whether it is working. I care about: - Clear explanations - Useful demos - Repeatable patterns over one-off wins - Governance that helps teams move safely instead of freezing them - Training that respects the developer's actual day-to-day work --- ## 🚀 Current themes A few areas I keep coming back to: - Copilot across the full SDLC - Agentic workflows and human review loops - MCP and tool-using agents - Custom instructions and repository context - AI governance for enterprise engineering teams - Measuring developer productivity and adoption signals - Keeping technical enablement content fresh as the platform evolves --- ## 🌱 Outside the day job I like learning, experimenting with tools, and building small things that help me understand bigger systems. Some projects are polished. Some are experiments. Most are part of the same habit: learn it, break it, rebuild it, explain it better. --- ## 🤝 Connect If you are thinking about GitHub Copilot adoption, AI-assisted software delivery, or how teams should prepare for agentic workflows, I am…

text: code-cargo organization CodeCargo CodeCargo is the AI-powered Internal Developer Portal for GitHub, purpose-built to orchestrate agentic workflows across the entire software lifecycle. United States of America # CodeCargo **The Control Plane for GitHub.** CodeCargo is the AI-powered Internal Developer Portal for GitHub, purpose-built to orchestrate agentic workflows across the entire software lifecycle. We help enterprises tame GitHub at scale — consolidating DevOps tooling, automating compliance, securing CI/CD, and giving developers self-service superpowers. [codecargo.com](https://codecargo.com) · [Documentation](https://docs.codecargo.com) --- ## What we build - **GitHub Migration** — Translate legacy pipelines from Jenkins, GitLab CI, CircleCI, and others into modern GitHub Actions with AI-assisted authoring. - **Workflow Guardrails** — Enforce security policies, compliance checks, and org standards across every workflow, with drift detection and audit evidence. - **CargoWall** — Kernel-level eBPF firewall for GitHub Actions runners. - **Developer Self-Service** — Multi-repo edits with GenAI, a private Actions marketplace, an agentic service catalog, and UI-callable automations. Built for enterprise scale. GitHub native. SOC 2 Type II. ## Open source We ship the security primitives we rely on in the open. - **[cargowall](https://github.com/code-cargo/cargowall)** — eBPF-based network firewall for GitHub Actions runners. Kernel-level egress filtering, dynamic DNS resolution, full process attribution, NDJSON audit logs. Audit and enforce modes. - **[cargowall-action](https://github.com/code-cargo/cargowall-action)** — The official GitHub Action. Drop one step into your workflow to lock down egress with hostname globs and CIDR rules: ```yaml jobs: cargowall-example: runs-on: ubuntu-latest permissions: id-token: write actions: read contents: read steps: - uses: code-cargo/cargowall-action@v1 with: # run in audit to learn what your job egress needs mode: audit ``` ## Get in touch - Website: [codecargo.com](https://codecargo.com) - Docs: [docs.codecargo.com](https://docs.codecargo.com) - Email: [[email removed]](mailto:[email removed])

text: Dynatrace organization Waltham, Boston # Dynatrace This organization is part of the Dynatrace Open Source Initiative. Projects are maintained by Dynatrace but if not stated differently are not officially supported. For more information about Dynatrace please visit [dynatrace.com](https://www.dynatrace.com/). ## Contact If you do have questions regarding any project within this organization, please open a GitHub issue for said project. If you do have general questions about open-source at Dynatrace, feel free to contact us at <[email removed]>. ## Default License We are using `Apache License 2.0` as our default License, see <https://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0>. > The Apache License 2.0 makes sure that the user does not have to worry about infringing any patents by using the software. The user is granted a license to any patent that covers the software. Through an in terrorem clause, this license is terminated if the user sues anyone over patent infringement related to this software. This condition is added in order to prevent patent litigations. - <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apache_License#Apache_License_2.0> ## ObsLab **ObsLab** is a collection of hands-on observability labs designed to help developers and practitioners learn by doing. The labs cover topics across Dynatrace and the broader observability ecosystem, including OpenTelemetry, log ingestion, release validation, performance testing, AI observability, Kubernetes, and application security. ### OpenTelemetry and data ingestion - [`obslab-otel-collector-data-ingest`](https://github.com/Dynatrace/obslab-otel-collector-data-ingest) Ingest logs, metrics, and traces using the Dynatrace OpenTelemetry Collector. - [`obslab-syslog`](https://github.com/Dynatrace/obslab-syslog) Ingest syslog data into Dynatrace using the OpenTelemetry Collector. - [`obslab-live-debugger-otel`](https://github.com/Dynatrace/obslab-live-debugger-otel) Explore live debugging and OpenTelemetry instrumentation. ### Reliability and performance - [`obslab-release-validation`](https://github.com/Dynatrace/obslab-release-validation) Use Grafana k6, Dynatrace business events, workflows, and Site Reliability Guardian to validate releases. - [`obslab-jmeter`](https://github.com/Dynatrace/obslab-jmeter) Explore integration between Apache JMeter and Dynatrace. - [`obslab-k6`](https://github.com/Dynatrace/obslab-k6) Stream Grafana k6 metrics into Dynatrace in a hands-on exercise. ### Troubleshooting - [`obslab-log-problem-detection`](https://github.com/Dynatrace/obslab-log-problem-detection) Detect problems in logs with Dynatrace. ### AI observability - [`obslab-llm-observability`](https://github.com/Dynatrace/obslab-llm-observability) Build an LLM-powered application and explore its observability with Dynatrace. ### Kubernetes - [`obslab-predictive-kubernetes-scaling`](https://github.com/Dynatrace/obslab-predictive-kubernetes-scaling) Explore predictive auto-scaling for Kubernetes workloads. ### Application security - [`obslab-unguard`](https://github.com/Dynatrace/obslab-unguard) Detect and block security vulnerabilities with Dynatrace. ### More hands-on demos In addition to the ObsLab exercises above, the `Dynatrace` organization contains several demonstration applications for different observability scenarios. github organization GitHub How people build software. United States of America ## Hey, this is us 👋 ![An illustration showing a variety of differently themed Octocats. Monuments from different cities are indicated in the background like the Space Needle, Berlin Fernsehturm and Transamerica Pyramid.](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/3369400/133268513-5bfe2f93-4402-42c9-a403-81c9e86934b6.jpeg) Yes, we are building GitHub on GitHub. In fact, we’ve been doing this since **October 19th, 2007**. That's when we made our first commit. Since then we pushed **over 2.5 million commits**, opened **over 1 million issues**, submitted roughly **650k pull requests** across **4357 repositories** from over **50 countries**. 🤯 But that's just us. We are proud to be part of the work of millions of developers, companies and robots across the solar system. 🪐 Yes, [Robots](https://github.com/readme/featured/nasa-ingenuity-helicopter)! ### 🍿 An interconnected community The open source community is the 💗 heart of GitHub and fundamental to how we build software today. See for yourself: - [GitHub Sponsors](https://github.com/sponsors) helped support more than **5k** individuals and projects around the world 🌍 - Open source projects on GitHub received a stunning **218 million** contributions 🚀 in the last year alone - **Every minute** a developer creates a new release 🏄 for a public project on GitHub Now that we are talking about the important things, ☝️ are you contributing to open source? Yes? Okay, you rock! 🎸 If not, we can help you get started! Open source software is made by people just like you. Learn more about [how to contribute](https://opensource.guide/). ### 🦦 Contributing to the ecosystem We contribute to the tools 🔧 we rely on to build and run GitHub, while also maintaining 🧙‍♂️ our own open source projects like: - [GitHub CLI](https://github.com/cli/cli) - A command line tool for GitHub - [GitHub Desktop](https://github.com/desktop/desktop) - A visual approach to using Git with GitHub - [Git Large File Storage](https://github.com/git-lfs/git-lfs) - A Git extension for versioning large files - [Primer](https://github.com/primer/css) - The GitHub design system ### 👓 Appendix See what's next on our [public roadmap](https://github.com/github/roadmap) ✨ and [let us know](https://github.com/github/feedback) if you have any suggestions. 🙇‍♂️ Oh, and by the way, we are always hiring talented, passionate people to [join our team](https://github.com/about/careers). 🙌
"Tell me more, I can't get enough!"
  • GitHub is built using mighty 🔨 open source technologies like Ruby on Rails, Go, Primer, React and Kafka among others.
  • The three open source projects GitHub members have most contributed 👩‍💻 to are:
    • Visual Studio Code
    • Ruby on Rails

text: launchdarkly organization LaunchDarkly Fast and reliable feature management for the modern enterprise Oakland, CA ## What is LaunchDarkly? LaunchDarkly serves a suite of tools that help you ship your code safer, faster, and more effectively with whatever language and frameworks you use today. ## How can LaunchDarkly help you? - _Feature flags_ let you reduce the risk of releasing new features by rolling them out progressively across subsets of your users over time. - _Guarded releases_ monitor the performance of flag releases and configure LaunchDarkly to take action on the results. - _AI Configs_ help you customize, test, and roll out new large language models (LLMs) within your generative AI applications. - _Experimentation_ lets you validate the impact of features you roll out to your app or infrastructure. You can measure things like page views, clicks, load time, infrastructure costs, and more. ## Explore LaunchDarkly: - [Sign up for a free developer account](https://app.launchdarkly.com/signup) - [Read our documentation](https://launchdarkly.com/docs) - [Join our Discord community](https://discord.com/invite/launchdarklycommunity)

text: OpenHomeFoundation organization Open Home Foundation The Open Home Foundation fights for the fundamental principles of privacy, choice, and sustainability for smart homes. Switzerland # Open Home Foundation The **Open Home Foundation** fights for the fundamental principles of **privacy**, **choice**, and **sustainability** for smart homes. And for every person who lives in one. It does this by supporting the development of open-source projects, and open connectivity and communication standards. A big part of our work is the ownership and governance of over 240 projects, open standards, drivers, and libraries that support the realization of the open home. Some are small projects to solve simple problems. Others represent major efforts to create open standards, prevent vendor lock-in, and protect privacy. Many are being used well beyond the smart home space. And we’re pretty proud of that. You can find all of our projects, standards, drivers and libraries in the following repositories: [home-assistant](https://github.com/home-assistant), [esphome](https://github.com/esphome), [zigpy](https://github.com/zigpy), [bluetooth-devices](https://github.com/bluetooth-devices), [home-assistant-libs](https://github.com/home-assistant-libs), [improv-wifi](https://github.com/improv-wifi), [piper](https://github.com/rhasspy/piper/), [wyoming](https://github.com/rhasspy/wyoming).

text: ossf organization Open Source Security Foundation (OpenSSF) OpenSSF is a community of software developers and security engineers who are working together to secure open source software for the greater public good. San Francisco, CA [OpenSSF](https://openssf.org/) is committed to working both upstream and with existing communities to advance open source security for all. We foster collaboration, establish best practices, and develop innovative solutions to secure the development, maintenance, and consumption of open source software. OpenSSF is part of the nonprofit [Linux Foundation](https://linuxfoundation.org/). - Visit our Projects page (https://openssf.org/projects/) ## Working Groups: - [AI/ML Security](https://github.com/ossf/ai-ml-security) - explore the security risks associated with AI and ML and their impact on open source - [Belonging, Empowerment, Allyship, & Representation](https://github.com/ossf/wg-bear) - foster a more diverse and inclusive cybersecurity workforce - [Best Practices for Open Source Developers](https://github.com/ossf/wg-best-practices-os-developers) — provide awareness, education, and guidance about security best practices - [Global Cyber Policy](https://github.com/ossf/wg-globalcyberpolicy) - collaborate on cybersecurity-related legislation, frameworks, and standards - [Securing Critical Projects](https://github.com/ossf/wg-securing-critical-projects) — identify and help secure critical open source projects - [Securing Software Repositories](https://github.com/ossf/wg-securing-software-repos) — strengthen the security posture of software repositories - [Security Tooling](https://github.com/ossf/wg-security-tooling) — identify and provide state of the art, globally accessible security tools - [Supply Chain Integrity](https://github.com/ossf/wg-supply-chain-integrity) — ensure the provenance of open source code - [Vulnerability Disclosures](https://github.com/ossf/wg-vulnerability-disclosures) — enable efficient vulnerability reporting and remediation For any questions, concerns, reports, etc., please email [email removed]. ## Get Involved - Join the [OpenSSF Slack](http://slack.openssf.org/) - Subscribe to the [OpenSSF monthly newsletter] (https://openssf.org/sign-up/) - Join one of the [OpenSSF Mailing Lists](https://lists.openssf.org/g/main/subgroups) - Attend Working Group, Special Interest Group (SIG), and Project meetings, which can be found on our [Community Calendar](https://calendar.google.com/calendar?cid=czYzdm9lZmhwNWk5cGZsdGI1cTY3bmdwZXNAZ3JvdXAuY2FsZW5kYXIuZ29vZ2xlLmNvbQ) - For more ways to participate, visit our [Get Involved page](https://openssf.org/getinvolved/) ## Membership We encourage all individual contributors to work with their employers to become members. We aim to grow an active, healthy community of contributors, reviewers, and code owners. Learn more about the requirements and responsibilities of membership in our [Membership page](https://openssf.org/join/) or see [current members](https://landscape.openssf.org/).

Amsterdam, Netherlands ### Hey, I'm Sam I'm a Senior Software Engineer at [GitHub](https://github.com), building tools that help developers work with AI. ## Current Focus **[GitHub MCP Server](https://github.com/github/github-mcp-server)** - I build and maintain GitHub's official Model Context Protocol server, enabling AI agents to interact with GitHub. **[Model Context Protocol](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/modelcontextprotocol)** - Contributing to the MCP specification including SEPs for [Tool Resolution](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/modelcontextprotocol/pull/1862) and [Trust Annotations](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/modelcontextprotocol/pull/1913), plus security docs on [session hijacking](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/modelcontextprotocol/pull/641). ## Talks & Appearances [VS Code Live: Extending Agent Mode](https://youtu.be/T44T55wvDD0) - Interview and live demo [The Context: GitHub & Microsoft Special](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rtht8dbwe5U) - Live demo with MCP community hosts [LastMile AI: MCP at Hyperscale](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0d9TR91iLx0) - Building servers that serve millions ## Projects [reMarkable MCP Server](https://github.com/SamMorrowDrums/remarkable-mcp) - An MCP server for accessing reMarkable tablet data **MCP Starter Templates** - Getting started with MCP? I've created starter templates: - [mcp-python-starter](https://github.com/SamMorrowDrums/mcp-python-starter) - [mcp-go-starter](https://github.com/SamMorrowDrums/mcp-go-starter) - [mcp-typescript-starter](https://github.com/SamMorrowDrums/mcp-typescript-starter) ## Open Source I enjoy contributing across the ecosystem: - [Participate in issues](https://github.com/search?q=commenter%3ASamMorrowDrums+-user%3ASamMorrowDrums&type=issues) to help get them closed - Contribute [documentation](https://github.com/search?q=author%3ASamMorrowDrums+type%3Apr+is%3Amerged+docs+OR+documentation&type=pullrequests) to projects - Work in [Rust](https://github.com/ruffle-rs/ruffle/pulls?q=is%3Apr+author%3ASamMorrowDrums), [Go](https://github.com/github/github-mcp-server/pulls?q=is%3Apr+author%3ASamMorrowDrums+is%3Amerged), [TypeScript](https://github.com/palantir/plottable/pull/3087), [Python](https://github.com/SamMorrowDrums/remarkable-mcp), and more ### [Read my blog →](https://sam-morrow.com/blog)

Join CoreStory's Charath Ranganathan for a Microsoft Reactor webinar on why "almost right" code costs the most, and what grounding AI in your actual system returns. 📅 September 1 | 11 PM PT 🔗 Register: https://lnkd.in/gr-7Ntcs #AI #DeveloperProductivity #MicrosoftReactor AI can only go so far when no one fully understands the system it’s working in. Join CoreStory’s Ray Ploski for a Microsoft Reactor webinar on how persistent system intelligence can help teams modernize complex codebases with greater speed and confidence. 📅 August 25 | 11 AM PT 🔗 Register: https://lnkd.in/eVks8j3a #AI #LegacyModernization #MicrosoftReactor For the research-minded — CoreStory Frontier's PATOIS study is out. The question: when an AI agent is working through a multi-step task, does it help to attach instructions to each response the system sends back? Or does the agent already know what to do? We ran 600 trials across five conditions. The answer splits cleanly in two. Tell the agent something it could never have worked out on its own — like the random string a server hands back meaning "this is where page two starts" — and it uses it every time. 30 out of 30. Leave that string out, and it fails every time. 0 out of 30. Tell the agent something any competent engineer already knows — how paging works, when to stop, when to lock — and nothing changes. The model already had it right. We also tried a stricter, more structured format for those instructions. Identical behavior, 38% more output. You pay for the formality and get nothing back. So the takeaway isn't "write longer prompts." It's narrower: send the agent the facts it cannot infer, and make everything else earn its place. Full write-up: frontier.corestory.ai

text: Develocity affiliation Develocity is the universal toolchain and artifact observability platform for AI-driven software delivery. As the context engineering layer for software delivery, it brings governance to keep AI-driven delivery accountable and auditable, and efficiency to keep it fast without runaway costs. Built by the same team behind Gradle Build Tool, one of the most widely used build systems in the world. The context engineering layer for AI-driven software delivery. Software Development LinkedIn size range: 51-200 employees 2010 Context Engineering AI-Driven Software Delivery Toolchain Observability Artifact Observability AI Governance Software Supply Chain Security Platform Engineering Developer Productivity Developer Productivity Engineering Engineering Effectiveness DevOps Build Cache Test Distribution Predictive Test Selection Build Scan CI/CD Acceleration Flaky Test Detection AI Agents Gradle Maven A fresh runner downloads hundreds of megabytes before any test runs. It doesn’t have to. Playwright pulls browsers, Cypress grabs its runner, pip fetches wheels every time. That’s minutes per job, and stalled downloads can fail it outright. More agents mean more jobs, more waiting, more risk. Develocity 2026.3 caches these artifacts nearby, serving pip, Playwright, and Cypress packages from a local edge node instead of the open internet. Python setup is now up to 40% faster against a cold cache. One step in GitHub Actions or Jenkins: https://lnkd.in/gimWHz9K #ShipNote #Develocity Your agent passes the check, but bugs still slip through. More eyes on the review won't fix it. When your AI writes both the code and its own tests, a green checkmark doesn't mean it's right. It might write tests that pass for the wrong reasons, or just delete a test that was failing. Teams trust and approve passing builds and bugs slip through. With agents now pushing more code than people, the more you scale, the larger the scope of the problem. The fix? Test every change against your real regression suite, the tests your agent didn't write. Lock it from editing existing tests during a fix (it can still add new ones). Hans Dockter explains why even smarter models won't solve this: https://lnkd.in/ghgP88Ue #FromTheFounder #ContextEngineering #Develocity Your builds pass, but they rerun every downstream test without telling you why. A cache key depends on a task's inputs. Change just two bytes in an early output, and every key downstream changes too. So tests, analysis, and packaging all run again; and since the build passes, the team doesn’t look. You pay for it on every build: in CI costs and waiting time. More agents mean more builds, so the waste compounds. A cache miss without a failure only shows up when you compare builds. Build Scan Comparison does that, it puts two builds side by side and shows exactly what input changed. That’s how we traced one issue to javac itself: it was writing the same class differently on different machines. Read the blog: https://lnkd.in/gsws-g6e #WhatWeLearned #Develocity Your AI agents write code fast, then wait on CI. Why? Each failed build is a do-over. You pay for the compute, and the fix can't ship. A Bluesky dev captured the pain perfectly in that screenshot. Scale this up and the problem gets worse. More agents mean more changes in the queue, longer waits, bigger bills, and all that AI speed lost to idle time. The solution? Do less work each run. A build cache skips unchanged tasks so a one-line fix doesn’t rebuild everything, and test selection runs only what’s affected. DX’s new capabilities include a way to capture information that helps teams: - Identify friction in areas like customer access, priority stability, and engineering collaboration - Quantify its impact through metrics like requirements rework, implementation fidelity, and meeting time - Understand AI adoption and impact, including time saved using AI tools This is a significant step toward measuring and improving productivity across the PDLC. Learn more: https://lnkd.in/gCRFnQ_M Your AI agent is only as good as the context it can reach. If critical knowledge isn't documented, permissions block access, or instructions are cluttered with irrelevant information, agents are left to guess, and will often confidently produce the wrong result. Good context requires three preconditions: the information has to exist, the agent has to be able to access it, and what it receives has to be relevant to the task at hand. Read the full CAFE(S) paper to learn more about what good context looks like. Link in the comments. 94% of AI token consumption is now spent re-reading context. In our latest Q3 AI Impact Report, we found that cache-read tokens reached 94% of the total token mix over the past four quarters, while output tokens shrank. The data suggests AI spend is growing because the background context required to produce code is ballooning, not because models are generating more code. Median PR size is up 122% year-over-year. Teams have more code to review and the same review capacity. Published today, our Q3 AI Impact Report points to that volume as the main reason why first reviews are taking longer. Our research team suggests two other factors that could also be slowing first reviews: 1. AI-generated changesets take more effort to review, which ties up reviewers and pushes everything else back in the queue. 2. Reviewers hesitate to pick up large, unfamiliar, or AI-generated diffs because they're worried about missing a bug that's hard to spot. Juniper Square will be there in full force! Last week, Juniper Square brought some relaxation to the back office. At the IMN Real Estate GP/LP Summit, we introduced Fund Paradise: our take on what fund operations can feel like when capital calls, reporting, reconciliation, and the rest of the manual work run on one connected platform. Plenty is changing across private markets, and the teams navigating it don't have time to be weighed down by the work that happens behind the scenes. Of course, it wasn't all play as we also tackled some very real questions facing the industry. Todd Rich unpacked for us the growing disconnect between where real estate equity is flowing and where capital is needed, while a group of operators shared how they’re deciding what to build, what to buy, and where AI is actually making their teams better. Thanks to everyone who stopped by Fund Paradise, joined our sessions, and spent time with the Juniper Square team. Back to reality (for now). Yesterday I spent 6 hours with 50 leaders across institutional real estate talking about AI. This was part of the inaugural NAREIM Innovation Summit. While the detailed conversations are always confidential at NAREIM, a few themes emerged that are worth sharing: 1. We have moved from AI being a novelty to driving NOI 2. The technology is the worst it will ever be today and it's already capable of executing some of the most complex and nuanced tasks 3. Changing behaviors is far more difficult than changing technology - people across the board are very resistant to change 4. Leadership MUST come from the top. As AI moves deeper into workflows and agents, the conversation needs to move beyond licences, tokens and even time saved. 👉 AI should increasingly be managed as variable enterprise capacity, not simply as an incremental technology cost. 👉 This is where architecture, finance and governance meet. The more important question is: where should we allocate intelligence, and what business outcome are we getting in return? That could mean greater capacity, faster cycle times, better quality, lower risk or new growth. The point isn’t simply to make AI cheaper. IT Services and IT Consulting LinkedIn size range: 2-10 employees Utrecht Utrecht, NL cargo (libnix) is a fork of cargo with nix built in as a build backend. three releases later 🦀❄️ here is what changed between libnix-1.87.0+v1 and +v3: 🔌 talking to the nix-daemon directly: cargo no longer runs nix build as a subprocess. it speaks the nix worker protocol, so it knows exactly which crate failed, which ones were skipped and which ones came from a binary cache. 📋 build output that reads like cargo: the log renderer is now part of cargo. it prints Compiling / Downloading lines, rustc diagnostics, build logs for failed crates, a correct progress line and the evaluation time. ⚡ parallel builds again: build script flags are no longer read at evaluation time, so nix schedules independent crates in parallel. 📦 crates live in the nix store: in nix mode cargo never downloads a crate itself. the nix-daemon fetches them once (or substitutes them from cache.nixos.org ), and cargo and the nix build share the same store paths. ~/.cargo/registry stays empty. 🧊 flakes via IFD, no vendoring: cargo build write-nix-buildsystem --out-dir generates the build system from the local source. for offline builds the crates.io index is no longer needed: the crate tarballs are computed from Cargo.lock in plain nix and passed in as inputs. no network, no importCargoLock. 🛠️ smaller things: nixpkgs 26.05, cargo --version says +libnix, nix develop works better, and there are clearer safety checks. it's still slower than vanilla cargo, but sandboxed, shared and cached builds plus readable logs make it a pleasant way to build rust with nix. 👉 https://lnkd.in/eDrbN4df #nix #rust #cargo #opensource We’re proud to sponsor NixCon 2026! Software Development LinkedIn size range: 10,001+ employees Raleigh, NC 1993 cloud computing hybrid cloud management Linux open source virtualization storage middleware containers mobile OpenStack Raleigh, NC, US This is me at 11 years old, sporting a red fedora for a photo I thought I'd never use again. It's We Are Red Hat Week. A celebration of our open source culture and an opportunity to look back on our history. The story of our hat [1] is worth a read if you're unfamiliar. This week I've been reflecting on what the hat means to me... Raised in the mountains of Western North Carolina, my education was rooted in Outward Bound and Expeditionary Learning design principles and models at a small public charter school. Curiosity, collaboration, hands-on discovery, and leaning into challenges shaped how I navigate the world. I learned that real growth happens outside comfort zones, that everyone has something valuable to contribute, and that the best work happens when people build things together. In sixth grade, I won a class locker-decorating contest with a photo of myself wearing a red fedora in a contemplative pose with witty thought bubbles above my head. Many years later, I found my way to Red Hat. A company and community anchored in openness, collaboration, curiosity, and meritocracy. Red Hat’s culture of shared ownership, learning from one another, and empowering humans echoes the very educational philosophies that shaped me. To me, the hat serves as a bridge, symbolizing the shared ethos of growth, trust, and collective effort that unites the principles of our Open Organization, Outward Bound, Expeditionary Learning, and how I strive to move through the world. So, maybe my path to Red Hat wasn't accidental. Or maybe the universe just knew that an 11 year old in a red fedora was destined to find her people in open source. Either way, I think the photo makes a pretty compelling case. [1] https://lnkd.in/e9VHMkFy Tired of false alerts overwhelming your security team? Red Hat researchers and Purdue University engineers have created VEX-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating large language models (LLMs) in assessing software supply chain vulnerability triage. VEX-Bench provides a clear, transparent method to gauge LLMs' ability to accurately reason about vulnerability advisories and perform effective triage. https://red.ht/4xSld1X It’s We Are Red Hat Week, a yearly celebration of open source culture. Now that I’m entering into my 10th year at Red Hat, forgive me for waxing a little philosophical about what that culture means to me. When I was young, I used to think I had the best creative ideas. I was pushy and a bit arrogant. If things didn’t turn out well, I blamed the execution of others, not my ideas. But as I’ve matured, I see collective participation as an antidote to that creative hubris. Other people’s ideas can be incredibly helpful even if they might slow things down. I’ve long felt there’s a universal war between consolidation and decentralization. From governments to industries to city planning to galaxies, there’s always a push-pull in one direction or the other. I know there are pros and cons to each, but overly centralized systems always seemed more of a problem to me than dispersed ones (maybe that’s just my inherent mistrust of authority). Centralized systems are easier to control, there’s faster decision making and rapid response, and they can eliminate duplicated efforts. But the risk of group think, rigidity and blind spots is really high. Decentralization is messier. There…

Computer and Network Security LinkedIn size range: 51-200 employees San Francisco 2020 Software Security Software supply chain Open source software Application Security Cybersecurity Software Composition Analysis (SCA) San Francisco, US Attackers were stealing secrets from LiteLLM's GitHub org 11 days before they published the malicious litellm 1.107.0 release. Socket 's Threat Research Team recovered two malicious workflows that ran in BerriAI/litellm on October 10 and October 12. Both runs succeeded. Neither left a trace in the repo's normal history. The technique: • Cut a throwaway branch (ci-tmp-<hex>) from a legitimate recent commit • Push one commit adding .github/workflows/ cache.yml , titled "ci: bump cache config" • Let on: [push] fire in the upstream repo, where secrets resolve to real values • Base64 the secrets, POST them to webhook.site , and append || true so the run always reports success • Delete the branch the same day The October 10 run took six org-level secrets, including a GitHub token and a GitHub App private key. Two days later, a six-job workflow bound five real GitHub Environments to unlock their secrets and took 14 more. No overlap with the first set. Reconnaissance, then collection. Among the 20 secrets: OpenAI, Anthropic, and Bedrock keys, Postgres and Redis credentials, a GitGuardian key for the secret scanner that would surface this activity, and Playwright session state that grants Linear access without a password or MFA. Deleting the workflow didn't erase the evidence. Environment deployment records survive. One is still marked Active, deployed from ref ci-tmp-4d8517. Socket contacted the LiteLLM team as soon as we found this and coordinated publication with them. LiteLLM has since published its own attack-chain investigation. It traces initial access to a key accidentally committed to a public repo in May and never revoked, and says its audit logs link the GH_TOKEN stolen on October 10 to approval of the October 21 release. Thanks to the LiteLLM team for working with us. What we can't confirm: whether October 10 was the start, whether more cycles ran before October 21, or whether the collectors received the data. If you run GitHub Actions, check your environment deployment history and Actions metrics for workflows you don't recognize, especially runs from branches that no longer exist. Full analysis and IOCs by Socket: https://lnkd.in/egxhpxub 🚨 New investigation: Socket found malicious LiteLLM workflows running 11 days before the attack, targeting 20 secrets including GitHub, cloud, and AI credentials. After our disclosure, LiteLLM linked a stolen token to approval of the malicious release. https://lnkd.in/ecYJAe6r Good news, everyone! text: Standard Agents affiliation Domain-specific agents running on your infrastructure. Professional tooling for the agentic era. AgentBuilder is developer tooling for building domain-specific AI agents (DSAs). There’s a misconception that the goal with agents is full lights-out. Code written, tested, deployed, maintained... no humans needed. I don't have that same desire for it. We run a lights-out operation at Swamp for ops and reactive work. Alerts come in, the system figures out what’s going on, handles it or escalates. That works because we’ve already done the thinking about what should happen. The system knows where to stop. Product work though? A small team build Swamp, none of us write code, and we’re still arguing about what to build and how it should work. Not reviewing diffs. Arguing about whether a feature belongs, whether the approach is right, whether we’ve thought about what happens when a user hits the edge we didn’t plan for. That taste is what we care about greatly! This is why I don't want to push toward full autonomy. A ticket like “add a retry command” looks ready to go. Then you start asking whether retry means restart from scratch or resume from the failure, what happens to infrastructure the first run created, whether the workflow definition might have changed since. We built three agent memory systems. The most expressive one wasn't the most useful. First, a list of user-scoped facts. Four tools, text snippets, and recall returned everything you had ever saved. Useful for personal preferences, but a poor fit for shared project knowledge. Only a handful of power users used it. Second, a general knowledge graph. Nodes, edges, JSONB metadata, and arbitrary SQL so agents could experiment freely. They got surprisingly good at SQL. They also spent their turns on database mechanics instead of the memory task: integrating one thread summary took dozens of turns. Third, a tree. One table, an ltree path per memory, and tools for working with it. Agents still chose what to remember, where to put it, and how to search. But saving a summary and establishing its place in the hierarchy usually took one tool call. The lesson wasn't that trees beat graphs. It was that flexibility can give agents more work without helping them do the job. Let agents decide what to remember and retrieve. Don't make them invent edge semantics and operate the database to do it. https://lnkd.in/euPzk8Fn #AIAgents #PostgreSQL #RAG #OpenSource IIoT ingest on PostgreSQL has a failure mode that stays hidden until the day it matters. A remote site drops its uplink. The cause is someone else’s ticket. The backlog is yours. The sensors don’t care - they keep reading for six hours. Then the link comes back and all of it arrives at once. That’s when you find out two things you never tested. Whether those rows land once or twice. And what happens to every other site while that one pushes six hours of backlog through the same pipe. Most teams learn both answers in production. They need one exploitable path. It’s Cybersecurity Awareness Month, and this year’s theme is “Don’t Make It Easy for Them.” I wrote a piece for the XBOW blog applying it to application security. In my conversations with security teams, the same five gaps come up again and again: 1️⃣ Long gaps between tests. Apps ship new features, endpoints and permission changes every week. An annual pentest can’t keep up. 2️⃣ Backlogs with no validation. Thousands of scanner findings, and nobody knows which ones can actually be exploited. 3️⃣ Too little testing of auth, authz and business logic. These are the flaws that matter most, and predefined scans usually miss them. 4️⃣ Fixes closed without checking. A closed ticket isn’t proof. Patching one endpoint can leave the same access open through another. 5️⃣ Rigid testing. Real attackers adapt and chain small weaknesses together. Checklists don’t. The fix isn’t more headcount. Focus testing where change and business risk are highest, prioritize by proven exploitability, and retest every fix. Autonomous pentesting can take human expertise much further without a matching jump in manual effort. Which of these five shows up most in your org? text: Zed Industries affiliation We’re Zed Industries, a small and passionate team with a vision for building the world’s best text editor—for you, and for your team. Zed isn’t our first editor. It’s the culmination of more than a decade of experience building tools for developers. We created the hackable text editor, Atom, and the pioneering software platform that launched an entirely new generation of desktop apps, Electron. We also built Tree-sitter, an advanced syntax parsing framework used by the most popular editors in the world. Building tools that matter is in our DNA. Now, we’re building something new again with that same drive and a new vision. We believe the best software is handcrafted, with unparalleled attention to detail. We believe software development is better when it’s a shared experience. We believe there’s a better way to write software—and this is just the start of the adventure. Zed is a high-performance, multiplayer code editor from the creators of Atom and Tree-sitter. text: ZEISS Group affiliation ZEISS is an internationally leading technology enterprise operating in the fields of optics and optoelectronics. In the previous fiscal year, the ZEISS Group generated annual revenue totaling almost 12 billion euros in its four segments Semiconductor Manufacturing Technology, Industrial Quality & Research, Medical Technology, and Consumer Markets (September 30, 2025). For its customers, ZEISS develops, produces, and distributes highly innovative solutions for industrial metrology and quality assurance, microscopy solutions for the life sciences and materials research, and medical technology solutions for diagnostics and treatment in ophthalmology and microsurgery. The name ZEISS is also synonymous with the world's leading lithography optics, which are used by the chip industry to manufacture semiconductor components. There is global demand for trendsetting ZEISS brand products such as eyeglass lenses, camera lenses, and binoculars. With a portfolio aligned with future growth areas like digitalization, healthcare, and Smart Production and a strong brand, ZEISS is shaping the future of technology and constantly advancing the world of optics and related fields with its solutions. The company's significant, sustainable investments in research and development lay the foundation for the success and continued expansion of ZEISS' technology and market leadership. ZEISS invests 15 percent of its revenue in research and development – this high level of expenditure has a long tradition at ZEISS and is also an investment in the future. With over 46,600 employees, ZEISS is active globally in around 50 countries with more than 60 sales and service locations, around 40 research and development facilities, and 30 production facilities worldwide. title: FAQs
text: attendee-portal FAQs Where and when is Universe? Universe will take place on October 28 - 29, 2026 at [Fort Mason Center for Arts & Culture](https://fortmason.org/) in San Francisco, CA. Broadcast times and schedule will be announced in September. website Fort Mason Center for Arts & Culture What is your cancellation policy? To receive a refund on your order, please [contact us](https://airtable.com/appfOr0lGpRh28jTk/pagNqg817o65RLZ54/form) using the "Registration Support" category. Passes must be cancelled by 11:59pm on October 9. Refunds are not available after that deadline. contact us Are there sponsorship opportunities for GitHub Universe? We have a limited number of sponsorship opportunities available for GitHub Universe. To learn more, visit [event-sponsorship.github.com](http://event-sponsorship.github.com/) or [contact us](https://airtable.com/appfOr0lGpRh28jTk/pagNqg817o65RLZ54/form). event-sponsorship.github.com I’m traveling from outside the US. Can you help with my VISA application? Please consult our [visa specific FAQ's](https://static.rainfocus.com/github/universe26/static/staticfile/staticfile/Universe%202026%20VISA%20FAQ%27s_1781196981227001qEtb.pdf) for additional information about invitation letters and visa applications. other visa specific FAQ's How long will registration remain open? Registration opens in June and will remain open until passes sell out. Don't forget, if you can't make it in person you can still join virtually. Do you offer discounted passes or discounted pricing for students and non-profits? Yes, we offer group discounts for those that want to bring along their teams! If you purchase 4+ passes, you’ll receive 20% off each pass. We also have a limited number of discounted passes for students and non-profit organizations. Please [contact us](https://airtable.com/appfOr0lGpRh28jTk/pagNqg817o65RLZ54/form) for additional details. Is there a hotel room block for GitHub Universe? You bet! We’ve contracted with several hotels in the Fisherman’s Wharf area. You will have an opportunity to book a room at our conference rate during event registration, or from your Attendee Portal once registered. Other parties may solicit you to book at our contracted properties, but to ensure that you have a legitimate reservation at our special conference rate, rooms must be booked through our online conference portal. A credit card will be required to secure your reservation. Rates are subject to availability at time of booking. We recommend you reserve as early as possible. See hotel policies related to cancellation, early departures, etc. Do not contact the hotels directly to confirm, book, cancel, or amend your reservation. Are there speaking opportunities at GitHub Universe? Our call for sessions for Universe 2026 is now closed. Keep an eye out early next year for the Universe 2027 call for sessions — we’re always excited to hear new voices and ideas from across the community. Which airports are closest to San Francisco? San Francisco International Airport (SFO) is the closest major airport, an easy BART ride, or a 25-minute drive from downtown. Alternatively, the Oakland International Airport (OAK) is a 35-minute drive over the Bay Bridge and is also accessible by BART. Lastly, the San Jose International Airport (SJC) is a one-hour drive from the South Bay, accessible by Caltrain. What accessibility resources will be available at Universe? All sessions — with the exception of Ship and Tell, Sandbox sessions, and workshops — will have real-time captioning, and our main stage will include American Sign Language (ASL) interpretation. We’ll also have a dedicated quiet space and lactation room onsite. Fort Mason is a historic venue that has been retrofitted to meet ADA standards. If you have any accessibility needs or would like assistance planning your on-site experience, please connect with us by completing a [support form](https://airtable.com/appfOr0lGpRh28jTk/pagNqg817o65RLZ54/form) — we're happy to help!…

Analysis of LLMs vs Human Experts in Requirements Engineering Arxiv January 31, 2025 The majority of research around Large Language Models (LLM) application to software development has been on the subject of code generation. There is little literature on LLMs' impact on requirements engineering (RE), which deals with the process of developing and verifying the system requirements. Within RE, there is a subdiscipline of requirements elicitation, which is the practice of discovering and documenting requirements for a system from users, customers, and other stakeholders. In this analysis, we compare LLM's ability to elicit requirements of a software system, as compared to that of a human expert in a time-boxed and prompt-boxed study. We found LLM-generated requirements were evaluated as more aligned (+1.12) than human-generated requirements with a trend of being more complete (+10.2%). Conversely, we found users tended to believe that solutions they perceived as more aligned had been generated by human experts. Furthermore, while LLM-generated documents scored higher and performed at 720x the speed, their cost was, on average, only 0.06% that of a human expert. Overall, these findings indicate that LLMs will play an increasingly important role in requirements engineering by improving requirements definitions, enabling more efficient resource allocation, and reducing overall project timelines. Second, the intensifying, worldwide competition in all markets requires IT systems providing more agility, flexibility, scalability, robustness, and adaptivity in tackling daily businesses. Consequently, companies call for IT solutions with a high degree of autonomy - in order to manage themselves - as well as a high degree of decentralization - in order to provide the required, beneficial properties. Self-organizing emergent systems are generally acknowledged as a potential solution able to cover both of these requirements. They consist of many, simple elements (e.g. agents, servers, mobile devices, or robots), which have only partial or even no global system knowledge and make their decisions solely based on locally available information. The global coherent system behavior is achieved only by means of the local actions and interactions between the elements, each unaware of the system's goals. The problem-solving power of a self-organizing emergent system hence mainly resides in the interactions between its elements instead of the internal reasoning of individual elements. However, there exist several problems and challenges, which hinder the acceptance of self-organizing emergent systems by industry. This thesis tackles two of them: first, the design of efficient self-organizing emergent systems today is too complex, time-consuming, and costly. Second, an acceptable efficiency of self-organizing emergent systems during the operation cannot be guaranteed for all situations. This thesis presents several artifacts that on the one hand simplify the design of effective as well as efficient self-organizing emergent systems and on the other hand facilitate their efficient operation even in unforeseeable situations. text: AI1273D Generative AI and the future of development Since someone fed the first stack of punch cards into a computer to provide it a set of instructions, we've always been looking for ways to streamline development. title: Continuous AI: A new way to collaborate
summary: AI agents are transforming software development. Today, you can assign tasks to agents in GitHub.com, in VS Code, and on the command line via Copilot CLI. But what if you didn’t have to assign tasks to your agents? What if they could do work on your behalf, continuously in the…
text: BLD1143M Continuous AI: A new way to collaborate AI agents are transforming software development. Today, you can assign tasks to agents in GitHub.com, in VS Code, and on the command line via Copilot CLI. But what if you didn’t have to assign tasks to your agents? What if they could do work on your behalf, continuously in the background, without you having to ask? In GitHub Next, we’ve been exploring this idea, which we call “Continuous AI.” Just like continuous integration, Continuous AI is integrated into your development workflows and runs on GitHub Actions. But Continuous AI integrates LLMs and agents to do things that traditional continuous integration cannot – things that require judgement, that cannot be expressed as simple rules. They accelerate your team, not just individual developers. In this talk, we will present the concept of Continuous AI, describe what kinds of tasks it is useful for, and show many examples of real Continuous AI workflows we are using in our own projects and with our collaborators in the open source community. We’ll show you how you can write your own Continuous AI workflows using our open-source tool, Agentic Workflows, as well as try out examples from the community. This is a first look at experimental work from GitHub Next, GitHub's research and engineering team that focuses on shaping the future of software creation. If you’re curious about what’s coming next — and how to prepare for it — this session is for you. speaker VS Code abstract gazetteer Copilot CLI GitHub Actions Agentic Workflows

text: SEC1364W Secure more, stress less with a risk-based rollout of GitHub Advanced Security Regulators, customers, and auditors are raising the bar on software security — and organizations need to prove they have the right controls in place, without slowing down innovation. In this interactive workshop, you’ll jump into action to help “Acme Corp” recover from a breach by rolling out GitHub Advanced Security (GHAS) using a risk-based approach. You’ll work inside a live GitHub Enterprise Cloud (GHEC) organization to classify repositories by risk, apply the right security configurations, and automate governance with organization-wide rulesets. You’ll also see how this practical playbook helps you meet compliance requirements for frameworks like NIST SSDF, CRA, and SLSA — all while keeping your developers moving fast and focused on what they do best: building great software. facilitator GitHub Advanced Security title gazetteer GitHub Enterprise Cloud abstract

text: SEC1379D Say goodbye to static credentials with ephemeral SSH certificates Static credentials like Secure Shell (SSH) keys and personal access tokens (PATs) can create hidden security risks and headaches for teams. But there’s a better way. In this session, you’ll learn how to move beyond static credentials by using short-lived, ephemeral SSH certificates. We’ll show you how GitHub, combined with your identity provider and a certificate-issuing service, can eliminate the need for long-lived tokens — making access simpler, safer, and more scalable. You'll gain practical insights on how to improve your security posture, streamline credential management, and give developers a smoother, more secure experience. speaker

title: Avoiding the next supply chain disaster using GitHub and Gradle
summary: In this demo, we’ll show you how GitHub and Gradle are working together to improve supply chain security. You’ll learn how to enable the Gradle dependency-submission GitHub Action for your project, which leverages the GitHub Dependency Submission API to report all resolved…
text: SEC1384D Avoiding the next supply chain disaster using GitHub and Gradle In this demo, we’ll show you how GitHub and Gradle are working together to improve supply chain security. You’ll learn how to enable the Gradle dependency-submission GitHub Action for your project, which leverages the GitHub Dependency Submission API to report all resolved dependencies, not just those declared in your build files. This integration helps you and Dependabot identify and remediate vulnerabilities more efficiently at scale, which leads to more accurate security alerts, faster remediation, and a smoother workflow for securing your builds. Finally, we’ll explore how to use a Gradle Build Scan® and Develocity to discover even deeper insights. speaker Gradle title gazetteer Dependabot abstract

text: SEC1385B Navigating the wild seas of open source license compliance These days, every codebase relies on open source software (OSS). From testing tools to utility libraries and whole frameworks, using OSS accelerates development velocity and lets you focus on the parts of your app that really matter. But every package you use comes with its own license, and some licenses can introduce compliance or legal risk in unexpected ways. What are licenses, how do they work, and how can you navigate the wild seas of OSS licensing to make the best use of open source, while still keeping your project compliant and secure? In this session, we'll talk through all of this and more. speaker

title: Shut the context window! You're letting the tokens out

text: BLD1312D Shut the context window! You're letting the tokens out GitHub Copilot builds context from your open files, related code, and conversation history before every interaction, but most developers never see how much that payload grows. Understanding that mechanism is the difference between sharp output and token bloat. In this session, Dylan McCarthy shows how Copilot constructs context in practice, demonstrates the developer habits that quietly inflate token usage, and walks through focused workflows that produce better results with less overhead. Dylan will also demo lightweight GitHub-native guardrails that help teams catch overly broad changes before they merge. You'll leave with a mental model of context mechanics and practical patterns you can apply immediately. speaker GitHub Copilot abstract gazetteer

title: A pixel dog that writes songs: Lessons from my first MCP server
summary: It’s 2 a.m. You’re deep in a solo coding session. The terminal doesn’t care if you’re tired. Your IDE doesn’t notice you haven’t moved in an hour. But the golden retriever on your desk does. It tilts its head, nudges you with a Pomodoro timer, and when you finally ship that…
text: BLD1332H A pixel dog that writes songs: Lessons from my first MCP server It’s 2 a.m. You’re deep in a solo coding session. The terminal doesn’t care if you’re tired. Your IDE doesn’t notice you haven’t moved in an hour. But the golden retriever on your desk does. It tilts its head, nudges you with a Pomodoro timer, and when you finally ship that feature, it wags its tail and writes you a song. Yunika Liu isn’t a backend engineer; she builds products that make complex systems feel personal. But using GitHub Copilot and its MCP support, she shipped the first version of Coco in a week. Coco is a pixel-art golden retriever that now lives in a floating desktop window and on a 64×64 LED display, powered by an MCP server with nine tools, 10 pixel animations, WebSocket sync, and music composition. In this talk, Yunika brings Coco onstage and shows how anyone can build their own MCP server. The only prerequisite is an idea weird enough to be worth building. speaker MCP title gazetteer GitHub Copilot abstract

title: How GitHub taught Copilot to remember and when to forget
summary: Real developer work is sequential, but today's AI agents treat every task as a fresh start. What if Copilot could carry forward what it learned from your last session and drop what no longer applies? Alejandro Carderera De Diego and Cooper Nederhood built a benchmark from…
text: BLD1372B How GitHub taught Copilot to remember and when to forget Real developer work is sequential, but today's AI agents treat every task as a fresh start. What if Copilot could carry forward what it learned from your last session and drop what no longer applies? Alejandro Carderera De Diego and Cooper Nederhood built a benchmark from chains of real GitHub pull requests to test this and found a counterintuitive result: accumulated context can hurt performance. That finding powered two features now in development: Skill Forge and Copilot REM. In this session, you'll learn how both work, the measurable improvements they produce, and how to apply these principles to your own agent workflows. speaker Copilot title gazetteer

title: How to shift specifications from contracts to hypotheses
summary: Teams building agents and workflows powered by GitHub Copilot are inheriting a habit that quietly breaks: writing specifications as contracts. A traditional spec is binding. But AI doesn't work that way. The same prompt produces different outputs across runs, models, and…
text: BLD1398H How to shift specifications from contracts to hypotheses Teams building agents and workflows powered by GitHub Copilot are inheriting a habit that quietly breaks: writing specifications as contracts. A traditional spec is binding. But AI doesn't work that way. The same prompt produces different outputs across runs, models, and updates. If you over-trust the spec, you risk shipping features that "passed" while doing the wrong thing. Abandon specs entirely, and you lose control. In this session, Julio Arruda walks through two real production failures caused by this pattern, then introduces a working reframe. You'll leave with a three-practice checklist you can apply Monday. speaker GitHub Copilot abstract gazetteer

title: Code is the easy part: Building Home Assistant in the open
summary: "Building in the open" usually means one thing: code on GitHub. As engineers, the Home Assistant team will tell you that's the easy part. The hard work starts long before code — ideas, UX, design, architecture, the roadmap itself — and at Home Assistant, all of it happens on…
text: BLD1596H Code is the easy part: Building Home Assistant in the open "Building in the open" usually means one thing: code on GitHub. As engineers, the Home Assistant team will tell you that's the easy part. The hard work starts long before code — ideas, UX, design, architecture, the roadmap itself — and at Home Assistant, all of it happens on GitHub, across 20,000 contributors, hundreds of repositories, and a dozen GitHub organizations. This session shows how the Open Home Foundation runs its entire roadmap in the open, using what Issues, Projects, and Discussions have become over the last two years. You'll see how feature requests get debated in Discussions, how scoping happens in Issues with sub-issues and custom fields, and how a living roadmap in Projects lets anyone comment, steer it, pick up an item, and ship it. You'll also see the harder parts: being wrong in public and fixing it in public, and iterating with the community before any code is written. Because you don't have to be technical to contribute: every single person can, even with a comment, before a line of code exists. That's building in the open. speaker Home Assistant title gazetteer Open Home Foundation abstract

title: Sketching with code in the age of AI
summary: AI tools can now generate clean, functional output from a short prompt. The question is no longer how to write code, but how to understand what's been made. Qianqian Ye shows why sketching and thinking in code, beyond syntax, is essential for working with AI. Drawing from…
text: BLD1616M Sketching with code in the age of AI AI tools can now generate clean, functional output from a short prompt. The question is no longer how to write code, but how to understand what's been made. Qianqian Ye shows why sketching and thinking in code, beyond syntax, is essential for working with AI. Drawing from teaching creative coding at USC and leading the open source creative coding tool p5.js (built on GitHub), Qianqian demonstrates how creative coding builds the intuition to shape systems (not just prompt them) and what's lost when that iterative process disappears. John Maeda connects the dots between design, computation, and the creative judgment that AI can't replace. You'll leave with practical approaches for integrating AI into your workflow while keeping exploration and understanding intact. speaker p5.js abstract gazetteer

text: BLD1636S Goodbye, tutorial hell: AI guides and the new documentation layer For years, "developer education" has meant read the docs and hope. And most MCP servers are just API wrappers with extra steps. What if the server could teach instead? When an AI agent in GitHub Copilot or another MCP-compatible editor reads documentation through an opinionated MCP server, it stops giving generic advice and starts teaching the way your product is meant to be used. Claire Waters and Erin Mikail Staples show the difference live: you'll fork an open source reference server, install it in your editor, and watch agent behavior change side by side. text: BLD1638D Make your Postgres agent-ready: Branching, isolation, and safer shipping Giving agents access to real database infrastructure is risky: one wrong migration and production breaks. Database branching changes that. When your Postgres database supports instant, isolated branches, agents can safely experiment on real schemas and data without touching production. This means safer experimentation, faster shipping, and preview environments that spin up automatically. In this session, Andre Landgraf shows how branching and isolation work under the hood, how to set up agent-ready database environments using tools like MCP and GitHub Actions, plus a live demo of an agent managing a database branch end to end. You'll leave with a clear framework for making your own database infrastructure safe for agentic workflows. speaker MCP abstract gazetteer GitHub Actions

title: What happens between pressing Enter and getting a response from GitHub Copilot
summary: What are AI credits, and why does typing a few words consume thousands of them? Every GitHub Copilot interaction assembles a layered prompt before anything reaches the model. Most developers never see this process, which makes slow or irrelevant responses hard to diagnose. In…
text: BLD1640W What happens between pressing Enter and getting a response from GitHub Copilot What are AI credits, and why does typing a few words consume thousands of them? Every GitHub Copilot interaction assembles a layered prompt before anything reaches the model. Most developers never see this process, which makes slow or irrelevant responses hard to diagnose. In this session, Ken Muse and Mickey Gousset open up the pipeline: how VS Code builds these prompts, how the prioritization engine decides what stays in the context window and what gets silently dropped, and what real-world patterns look like in the debug logs. You'll leave knowing how to engineer your interactions for maximum signal and minimum waste. facilitator GitHub Copilot title gazetteer VS Code abstract

text: BLD1644H Building domain-specific AI agents for hardware reliability at NVIDIA GitHub Copilot catches surface-level issues. But what about hardware-specific constraints, firmware interactions, and system-level failures? For teams working on hardware-software systems, AI adoption is significantly more complex than in pure software environments. Maria Victoria Gromysch shares a practical framework developed at NVIDIA for integrating AI across the full engineering lifecycle: test generation at pre-commit, AI-assisted code review at commit time, and system validation in CI/CD. You'll also learn how to build domain-specific agents trained on internal logs and diagnostics, design a layered AI workflow, identify where general-purpose tools fall short, and close the feedback loop between production failures and model improvement. speaker NVIDIA title gazetteer GitHub Copilot abstract

title: The 2am RCA Agent: Architecting AI that investigates, not hallucinates
summary: At 2 am, an alert fires. You spend 90 minutes jumping between Grafana, Jaeger, and logs, correlating by hand, fighting confirmation bias, and writing the RCA doc backwards. Achin Gupta and Divya Mahajan built an agent that does this in seconds. Surprisingly, the LLM only…
text: BLD1657H The 2am RCA Agent: Architecting AI that investigates, not hallucinates At 2 am, an alert fires. You spend 90 minutes jumping between Grafana, Jaeger, and logs, correlating by hand, fighting confirmation bias, and writing the RCA doc backwards. Achin Gupta and Divya Mahajan built an agent that does this in seconds. Surprisingly, the LLM only handles 4 of 10 nodes. Signal fetching, BFS topology traversal, correlation, and scoring are fully deterministic, which means they’re auditable, replayable, and cheap. The LLM narrates the evidence rather than gathering it. In this session, you'll see the architecture, a live demo of an alert-to-RCA report in seconds, and the design principles that make the system trustworthy in production. All code is open source; the paper is published on Zenodo. You'll leave with a blueprint for building agents you can actually trust in the middle of the night. speaker Grafana abstract gazetteer

title: Write-only code: What happens to peer review when agents write the diffs
summary: Peer review was how engineers learned: juniors got sharper, seniors stayed honest. Then agents wrote the code, and reviewing each other turned into auditing machines. That's why it felt awful. On separate teams, Adam Jacob and Dylan Ratcliffe each found the same fix: stop…
text: BLD1776B Write-only code: What happens to peer review when agents write the diffs Peer review was how engineers learned: juniors got sharper, seniors stayed honest. Then agents wrote the code, and reviewing each other turned into auditing machines. That's why it felt awful. On separate teams, Adam Jacob and Dylan Ratcliffe each found the same fix: stop reviewing the code and review the plan a human writes before the agent builds. The human loop came back, and now they enjoy the work again. This talk is the two of them comparing notes and disagreeing hard on one thing: whether review stops mattering once software is no longer a garden you tend for people. You'll leave knowing how to move review upstream on your own team, with a clear view of what you keep and what you give up. speaker

title: Still open: How AI reshaped open source
summary: Open source isn't dying. It's being stress-tested in ways nobody anticipated. AI has accelerated contributions and made it easier than ever to ship code, but it's also introduced new questions about quality, governance, and what community means when bots can contribute at…
text: BLD1779P Still open: How AI reshaped open source Open source isn't dying. It's being stress-tested in ways nobody anticipated. AI has accelerated contributions and made it easier than ever to ship code, but it's also introduced new questions about quality, governance, and what community means when bots can contribute at machine scale. In this session, three leaders from the open source foundations community share what they're actually seeing: why AI makes open source more essential than ever, what maintainers are doing right now to handle the surge in AI-assisted contributions, and how foundations are updating governance structures that were built for human contributors. text: BLD1788B Agent-driven deployment beyond localhost, shared securely with your team (Sponsored) You and your agent just built something that works on your laptop. Now you want your team to use it, without exposing it to the whole internet or wrestling with passwords and credentials to lock it down. In this demo, you simply ask your agent to publish it, and it handles the rest: opening a pull request, deploying the app, and putting it behind private, identity-based access that only you can reach. Sharing it with your team is just as easy, and every change to who can get in is captured in a diff you approve. The result is a way to ship and share work that's private by default, where identity decides who gets access and the review trail records why. You'll leave knowing how agents can take your work from localhost to your team securely, without public URLs, shared passwords, or credentials to manage. speaker

This session explains the guardrails that make agent-powered workflows manageable, including scoped permissions, workflow governance, safe execution patterns, and review of agent contributions. Through architecture diagrams and workflow examples, you’ll see how teams can use agents to analyze code, maintain repositories, and handle repetitive work without giving them unrestricted access. text: BLD1919M Beyond the prompt: Building an AI that takes initiative Cameron Hamilton asked his AI assistant, HALIE, to connect the camera in his son's nursery. It turned that camera into a baby monitor he never asked for. When he asked it to automate business growth, it told him to meet customers in person. And when he audited its work, 38 of its 96 goals were about improving itself. How do you make a proactive agent dependable? This session walks through HALIE's three systems: anticipation (acting on needs without a prompt), self-evolution (improving its own tools and code), and metacognition (reviewing work and conversations to steer what comes next). Cameron covers experiments in making useful initiative repeatable, the architecture behind it, what it costs to run an agent on cheap models, and which decisions still need a human. You'll leave with practical ways to design agents that decide what to do next, learn from what helped, and earn more responsibility through measurable results. speaker

text: LDR1785D Auth for agents: How auth.md lets agents skip the sign-up form (Sponsored) Every AI agent hits the same wall: to act on a user's behalf, someone still has to create an account, generate an API key, and paste it into a config file. auth.md is WorkOS's open protocol for skipping that step. Services publish a lightweight auth.md file pointing agents to a standard discovery document. From there, an agent that already knows who its user is can exchange that identity for scoped, short-lived credentials to your API. No signup form, no copied API key, no separate developer console. In this live demo, WorkOS will show auth.md end-to-end: an agent discovering support for the protocol, asserting a user's identity, and getting back scoped credentials it can use immediately — plus what it takes to add auth.md support to your own API. You'll leave understanding how the protocol works under the hood, why identity-based credential exchange is safer than long-lived API keys, and how to publish your own auth.md file so any agent can authenticate to your API without a single copied secret. speaker

But it's a problem when you need to know exactly what your build reached out to. After an incident, can you say which URLs a workflow hit? Can you stop it from talking to anything you didn't approve? text: TRU1422H The O(1) patch: Securing the supply chain against AI-discovered zero-days AI models can now autonomously discover decades-old CVEs, which means the software supply chain has never been more fragile. When the next zero-day drops, scanning your infrastructure node-by-node with non-deterministic package managers is an O(n) problem: by the time you know where you're exposed, you're already too late. This session explores a different foundation. By shifting to deterministic package management — built on the principles of NixOS and nixpkgs — CVE detection and remediation become an O(1) lookup against a fixed, cryptographic manifest of exactly what's in your system. Instead of asking "are we affected?" and scanning to find out, you already know, instantly and provably. You'll leave understanding what "secure by construction" really means, how deterministic builds change your exposure model when a zero-day hits, and what it takes to move toward this approach in a real supply chain. speaker

summary: Vulnerabilities reach developers from two directions. New code arrives faster than ever, and better scanning uncovers old flaws in code merged long ago. Both usually land on a security tab, away from where you work. In this demo, we'll show how developers building with agents…
text: TRU2230D Keep vulnerabilities out of your codebase, without leaving where you build Vulnerabilities reach developers from two directions. New code arrives faster than ever, and better scanning uncovers old flaws in code merged long ago. Both usually land on a security tab, away from where you work. In this demo, we'll show how developers building with agents can move security ahead of the code. You'll see how to review what you and your agents just wrote, including uncommitted changes, and fix issues before a pull request exists. Then we'll bring your repository's existing alerts into the same place, where Copilot can explain them, turn a long list into a clear fix-first plan and help you fix them as you build. speaker Copilot abstract gazetteer
